Turn the following internal draft into a clear member notice. Remove repetition, preserve essential rules and distinctions, and keep volunteer details separate. Do not invent a confirmed reopening date.

The neighborhood tool library is preparing to move from its borrowed room at West Hall to the former bus office on Alder Street. The move is scheduled for June 8, but that date is a planning target rather than a promise to reopen. The new building still needs a final electrical inspection. We have booked the inspector for June 3 and expect a decision that afternoon. If the inspection identifies work that cannot be finished by June 7, the move committee will publish a revised reopening date. Please do not tell members that the new location is guaranteed to open on June 10.

Members can continue borrowing from West Hall through June 1. After that date, volunteers will pack the collection and reconcile its inventory. The return box outside West Hall will remain available through June 15, including during the closure. It accepts hand tools only. Large equipment, including the tile saw and lawn aerator, must be returned during the staffed collection window on June 6 from 4 to 7 p.m. A member who cannot attend that window should call the library to arrange a collection; we have not authorized volunteers to make private collection arrangements using personal phone numbers.

No late fees will accrue from June 2 through June 15. This temporary waiver applies to items already overdue as well as items due during the move. It does not erase fees assessed before June 2. The distinction matters because members sometimes understand a fee waiver to mean that their whole balance has disappeared. Volunteers should explain the dates calmly and refer disputed older charges to the coordinator. The coordinator can review a disputed charge, but a referral is not a promise that the charge will be removed.

At the Alder Street building, members will enter through the courtyard gate, not the glass door facing the street. The street door opens into a room leased to another tenant. The courtyard entrance has a shallow ramp and an automatic opener. An accessible parking space is marked beside the gate, although the painted route from that space to the ramp is still awaiting approval. We should describe the installed ramp and opener accurately without announcing that the entire access project is finished. The access team will inspect the route after the contractor returns.

Packing volunteers need to attend one orientation, either May 28 at 6 p.m. or May 30 at 10 a.m. Both sessions cover safe lifting, labeling, and the inventory scanner. People who attended last year’s general volunteer training must still attend this move orientation because the scanner workflow is new. Nobody is required to lift heavy equipment. Volunteers can choose seated labeling work, and a trained moving company will handle the heaviest machines. Mentioning the moving company should not imply that it will pack the whole collection; volunteer packing remains essential.

The communications group wants a notice that members can use without reading committee minutes. It should give the borrowing cutoff, explain where and when returns are accepted, and make clear that the reopening date depends on inspection. We have repeated those points in several meeting notes because they affect different teams, but the final notice should state each rule once in a useful place. The volunteer orientation information should appear in a distinct short section so members who are not helping with the move can skip it. We will send the notice on May 24 and update it after the inspection. Until that update, staff should continue to use conditional language about reopening.

Edit this report into a readable board brief with findings, evidence limits, and a recommendation. Keep the material distinctions; length may increase locally where needed for clarity.

The pilot for the shared community kitchen ran for eight weeks and involved fourteen small food businesses. Ten businesses attended at least six sessions, while four attended fewer because of illness, staffing shortages, or equipment conflicts. This report describes what the pilot showed and what it did not show. Attendance was useful evidence of demand among the participating businesses, but it was not a survey of every food business in the district. The recruitment list came mainly from the market association, which means home-based producers outside that network may be underrepresented.

Booking records show that the kitchen was reserved for 312 hours. Those are reserved hours, not verified hours of production. Staff observed several bookings that ended early, and the electronic door log failed during the third week. We therefore cannot calculate a reliable utilization percentage from the records available. The booking total is still useful for staffing estimates, provided it is labeled correctly. A slide prepared for an early sponsor meeting called all 312 hours productive use. That slide should not be treated as the final finding or repeated in the public summary.

The participant survey received eleven responses. Eight respondents said access to the kitchen helped them accept an order they otherwise would have declined. Two said it made no difference to orders, and one was unsure. These are self-reported responses, not audited sales results. We did not collect invoices, margins, or a comparison group. The findings support saying that several participants reported an operational benefit. They do not support a claim that the kitchen increased district revenue or that every participating business grew. The three nonrespondents may have had different experiences.

Cleaning was the clearest operational problem. Staff recorded nineteen occasions when a station needed additional cleaning before the next booking. Twelve involved the same oven, whose removable panels were difficult to access. It would be misleading to treat all nineteen as evidence of careless behavior by nineteen different businesses. The records do not identify nineteen distinct businesses, and the oven’s design may explain part of the problem. The equipment team has requested a safer cleaning demonstration from the manufacturer. Until that happens, staff should keep the oven’s turnaround buffer in place.

The pilot budget was $24,000, and recorded spending was $21,600. The apparent underspend is not money available for a new program. A refrigeration repair invoice is outstanding, and the contractor has not yet provided the final amount. The finance officer expects to close the pilot accounts after that invoice arrives. The board can discuss a second pilot now, but it should not describe the remaining $2,400 as confirmed savings. The next proposal should show both an operating budget and a reserve for equipment failures, which the first pilot budget did not separately identify.

Participants asked for evening slots and a clearer process for reporting broken equipment. Staff support testing one evening per week, subject to having two trained staff on site. The safety policy requires two staff whenever the kitchen is open, regardless of how many businesses have booked. A low-demand evening cannot operate with one person simply to reduce costs. The booking form should include a damage-report link, but submitting a report will not automatically cancel a booking or determine who pays for a repair. Those decisions remain with the kitchen manager after review.

Our recommendation is to design a second, smaller test focused on evening demand and reliable use measurement. It is a recommendation for board consideration, not approval to spend or extend leases. A second test would require an approved budget and confirmation that staffing can meet the two-person rule. We should retain the limits of the evidence while making the practical next steps easier to see. Repeating every qualification after every finding makes the report difficult to read; placing each limit beside its relevant finding should be enough.
